text.p: These are the leading stories in the Namibian press on Thursday.
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Tensions are running high among Namibian delegates at the CITES conference in Harare on the eve of a crucial vote, which could see Namibia, Botswana and Zimbabwe win major concessions in their bid to downlist their elephant populations.

- Attempts by the National Housing Enterprise (NHE) and suspended senior manager Alpheus Gaweseb to reach an amicable conclusion over an early retirement package have ground to a halt. The major issue after two months of negotiations is a severance package for Gaweseb as well as conditions laid down by the NHE for his retirement. Gaweseb, a whistle blower in the multi-billion dollar Kafutura Single Quarters Scam, has been suspended from the NHE since October last year on full monthly salary for apparently having brought the housing parastatal into disrepute.

- The tenders in the race for a new presidential jet for the Namibian government, have now begun a public campaign to present their various offers. The European Airbus Industry on Wednesday presented its plans to the media to offer the government a jet of between N$134 million and N$157 million as a replacement for the Falcon 900. It also offered Air Namibia an Airbus 340 for about N$512 million as a replacement for the Boeing 747 currently in use. On Wednesday it came to light than an American company tendering with a Gulfstream V, has offered to take the Falcon 900 as a trade-in at an amount of about N$70,7 million.

- The protest tour by two Himba chiefs, who are trying to lobby support against the Epupa hydro-electric scheme in Europe, has gathered momentum with the Dresdner Bank AG in Germany, mother bank of the Commercial Bank of Namibia, saying it will not supply financing for the project.

- According to statistics supplied by Agribank, the Ovitoto communal area near Okahandja is the most overstocked communal region in the country, Compared to its carrying capacity the area is stocked 168 percent, while the Otjimbingwe area lies at 120 percent. The Agribank has received numerous applications from communal farmers for loans to buy stud cows, but the bank can only consider applications if the farmer comes from an area that is stocked at under 70 percent of its carrying capacity. Of the 12 communal grazing areas only three meet this requirement.
